name: Flaky Tests
intent: Treat a test that passes and fails on the same code as a defect with a cause, because retries and quarantines make the build green and can hide a real, intermittent bug.
scenario: A 32-test suite runs 200 times. Four tests flake for ordinary reasons: shared state left by another test, the clock, and a fixed sleep waiting for a variable job. A fifth test hides a genuine race in the code that fails about 1 attempt in 20. The team compares doing nothing, retrying, quarantining, and fixing the causes.
problem: A flaky test is usually defined as one that passes and fails without a code change. The common reaction is to add a retry or move the test to a quarantine, and that reaction is where the trap is. A retry turns a red build green whatever the reason for the failure, including a real bug that only fails now and then. A quarantine removes the test from the gate, and the real bug leaves with it. From the outside a flaky test and an intermittent defect look identical: it failed, it passed on the second try. Only the cause tells them apart, so the real work is finding the cause, not making the colour of the build change.

howItWorks.title: Look for the usual causes
howItWorks.text: Most flakiness comes from four places. Shared state: one test leaves data behind that another test reads, so the result depends on order. Time: a test that depends on the clock fails near a boundary such as midnight or a minute change. Waiting: a fixed sleep or timeout that is shorter than a job sometimes takes. Concurrency or the environment: a race in the code or a slow network. The first three are defects in the test, the last may be a defect in the product.

howItWorks.title: Reproduce it by controlling the variable
howItWorks.text: Make the suspect variable explicit. Run the tests in a fixed or reversed order, or with a printed random seed, to expose order dependence. Replace the clock with one the test controls and set it to the edge. Replace the fixed sleep with a wait for the condition that matters. A flake you can reproduce on demand is a bug you can fix, and the seed lets you replay a failure exactly.

howItWorks.title: Fix the cause in the test
howItWorks.text: Give each test its own state and clean it up, inject the clock, and poll for the event with a generous limit rather than sleep for a guessed time. These fixes usually make the suite faster as well, since the polling wait ends as soon as the job does. After the fix, the test should fail only when the code is wrong.

howItWorks.title: Use retries and quarantine as a bridge, not a cure
howItWorks.text: A retry or a quarantine can keep a team working while someone fixes the cause, and some teams run them on purpose. The trade-off is plain: every retry lowers the chance that a real intermittent bug turns the build red, and a quarantined test no longer guards anything. Count and report both, so the bridge does not become permanent.

howItWorks.title: Tell a test flake from a product flake
howItWorks.text: If a test fails on the same code with no clear cause in the test, assume it might be a real bug, such as a race or a missing lock, until you show otherwise. Reproduce it many times in a loop with the seed noted. A failure that survives after the test is isolated is evidence about the product, and it is the failure you most want to see.

pros: Fixing causes makes the red build mean something again, and often makes the suite faster
A printed seed or fixed order turns a once-a-week failure into one you can replay
Retries and quarantine keep a team unblocked while the real fix is scheduled
Tracking the flake rate per test shows which tests cost the most trust
cons: Finding the cause of a flake can take longer than rewriting the test
Retries cost run time and slow the suite when many tests need them
Quarantined tests tend to stay quarantined, and the lost coverage goes unseen
Controlling the clock or the order means changing code and test structure
whenToUse: A build fails on re-run without a code change, and people have started to re-run by habit
A test fails only on a busy CI machine or only in a certain order
Deciding on a team policy for retries and quarantine
whenNotToUse: As a reason to delete tests that feel annoying: a flaky test may be the only one watching a real risk
To chase a one-off failure that has an obvious cause, such as a broken dependency
When tests exercise a real network service you do not control: isolate the dependency first, then judge the rest
pitfalls: A retry that makes a red build green also makes a real, intermittent bug turn green: in the model, 14 real failures were all hidden by 2 retries
Quarantining the flaky tests along with the one that is a real race, because it looked flaky too
A fixed sleep that works on a laptop and fails on a loaded CI machine
Tests that pass alone and fail in the full run because an earlier test left state behind
Letting a quarantine grow with no owner and no deadline, so the gate quietly guards less every month
Judging flakiness by the count of red builds and not by whether the failures were real

quiz.question: A test fails once in a while. Adding two automatic retries makes the build green. What is the main risk?
options: The suite becomes slower by exactly the number of retries.
The retries may use more memory than the original run.
A real bug that fails only now and then will pass on a retry, so it is never reported.
Retries turn passing tests into failing ones.
quiz.explanation: A retry cannot tell a bad test from an intermittent bug. A bug that fails 1 time in 20 is very unlikely to fail three times in a row, so it goes green and ships. Slower runs are a cost, but the hidden bug is the danger.

quiz.question: A test fails only when run right after another test that wrote to a shared table. Which fix goes to the cause?
options: Run the suite twice and take the better result.
Give each test its own data and clean it up, so order stops mattering.
Always run the writer test last.
Add a sleep before the failing test so the table settles.
quiz.explanation: The cause is shared state, so isolate it. Re-running or moving tests around hides the dependence, and a sleep does not remove it. Isolation also lets the tests run in any order or in parallel.

quiz.question: A test waits a fixed 18 ticks for a job that takes between 1 and 20. What is the better design?
options: Raise the wait to 19 ticks, which is almost always enough.
Make the test retry once when the wait expires.
Mark the test as flaky and ignore its result.
Wait for the condition to become true, with a generous upper limit as a safety net.
quiz.explanation: Polling for the condition ends when the job ends, so it passes whenever the job finishes and is faster on average. A longer fixed wait only moves the edge, and retrying or ignoring the test hides it.
